Name: Is Everything a Language?
Description: Semiotic candidates evaluated by formula — shows substrate-equality holds for non-CRUD ontologies too.

LanguageCandidates.summary_rich: The **taxonomy under examination**. Each row is a *candidate* — English, Python, A Coffee Mug, A Thunderstorm, Honeybee Waggle Dance, OWL/RDF — annotated with the predicates the operational definition of *language* turns on: `HasSyntax`, `IsParsed`, `HasLinearDecodingPressure`, `IsStableOntologyReference`, `CanBeHeld`, `HasIdentity`, `DistanceFromConcept`. The rulebook then *computes* which ones qualify and surfaces any disagreement between its prediction and the row's declared status as `PredictionFail`. Edit a predicate and the verdict flips the same instant.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Name of the language candidate being classified.

schema.name: IsLanguage
schema.Description: The test answer that is intended to match the Family Feud answer to be "correct".

schema.name: HasGrammar
schema.Description: Does this candidate have a Grammar?  Generally follows candidates that have syntax also have grammar.

schema.name: HasSyntax
schema.Description: Does this language candidate have syntax and/or grammar?

schema.name: CanBeHeld
schema.Description: Is this candidate physical/material.  I.e. could it at least theoretically "be held"?

schema.name: Question
schema.Description: Question that 100 random people could be asked, family feud style.

schema.name: PredictedAnswer
schema.Description: The predicted answer as the top most popular answer among those in the family feud polling pool.
schema.explanation_rich: **The operational definition of *language*, executed as a formula.** An eight-clause `AND` gate: a candidate counts as a language only if it has syntax, requires parsing, describes something (rather than *is* the thing), exerts linear decoding pressure, resolves to an AST, references a stable ontology, can't be physically held, and has no individual identity. Worked example: **English** passes all eight — `HasSyntax=TRUE`, `IsParsed=TRUE`, `DistanceFromConcept=2` (so `IsDescriptionOf=TRUE`), `CanBeHeld=FALSE`, `HasIdentity=FALSE` — so `PredictedAnswer` resolves to `TRUE`. **A Coffee Mug** fails six of eight and resolves to `FALSE`. Flip `HasSyntax` to FALSE on English and the same formula instantly demotes it. The definition is the code; the code is the definition.

schema.name: PredictionPredicates
schema.formula: =IF({{HasSyntax}}, "Has Syntax", "No Syntax") & " & " & IF({{IsParsed}}, "Requires Parsing", "No Parsing Neede") & " & " & IF({{IsDescriptionOf}}, "Describes the thing", "Is the Thing") & " & " & IF({{HasLinearDecodingPressure}}, "Has Linear Decoding Pressure", "No Decoding Pressure") & " & " & IF({{ResolvesToAnAST}}, "Resolves to AST", "No AST") & ", " & IF({{IsStableOntologyReference}}, "Is Stable Ontology", "Not 'Ontology'") & " AND " & IF({{CanBeHeld}}, "Can Be Held", "Can't Be Held") & ", " &IF({{HasIdentity}}, "Has Identity", "Has no Identity")

schema.name: PredictionFail
schema.Description: If the family feud answer does not match the chosen language candidates status then this explains what did not match. t also flags (in english) mismatch where a candidate is marked as BOTH open AND closed world which does not make sense.
schema.formula:
=IF(NOT({{PredictedAnswer}} = {{IsLanguage}}),
  {{Name}} & " " & IF({{PredictedAnswer}}, "Is", "Isn't") & " a Family Feud Language, but " & 
  IF({{IsLanguage}}, "Is", "Is Not") & " marked as a 'Language Candidate.'", "") & IF({{IsOpenClosedWorldConflicted}}, " - Open World vs. Closed World Conflict.", "")
schema.explanation_rich: **The falsifier audit — where the rulebook accuses itself.** This field stays empty whenever the formal prediction agrees with the declared `IsLanguage` status. The moment they disagree, it prints the disagreement in English. Worked example: **Falsifier B** satisfies the eight-clause predicate while its declared `IsLanguage` status is false, so this field prints that mismatch instead of hiding it. Add a NEIAL step to refine the definition, edit a predicate to flip the verdict, or accept the boundary case: every move is auditable.

schema.name: Category
schema.Description: The general high level category of the candidate.

schema.name: HasIdentity
schema.Description: Could this thing be assigned a guid, unique in the universe that would identify it globally?  Like a drivers license or social security number for a person.

schema.name: IsParsed
schema.Description: Is the knowledge/information encoded in a form that requires parsing before meaning can be extracted?

schema.name: ResolvesToAnAST
schema.Description: Is the knowledge/information encoded in a form that requires parsing before meaning can be extracted?

schema.name: IsOpenClosedWorldConflicted
schema.explanation_rich: **A row cannot be both open-world and closed-world at once.** This one-line `AND` is a *self-check* — if it ever fires, the curator has marked a candidate as simultaneously OWA (anything not asserted may still be true) and CWA (anything not asserted is false), which is incoherent. Worked example: **OWA & CWA Falsifier** is deliberately authored that way as a trap; this field resolves to `TRUE`, and the `PredictionFail` audit appends *"- Open World vs. Closed World Conflict."* to the row. The ontology refuses to lie quietly.

schema.name: HockettAssessedCount
schema.Description: How many of Hockett's design features this candidate has a published assessment for. Zero means nobody has assessed it, which is not the same as failing.

schema.name: HockettYesCount
schema.Description: How many assessed design features this candidate satisfies outright.

schema.name: IsHockettAssessed
schema.Description: TRUE once this candidate has at least one published design-feature assessment.

schema.name: HockettScore
schema.Description: The design-feature tally as text, reading "not assessed" rather than "0" when there is no published assessment. A hand-written Postgres function used to sum eleven bio_has_* columns that were never in the rulebook, so every candidate silently scored zero; this field replaces it.
schema.explanation_rich: **The rival definition's answer, next to this rulebook's own.** Where `PredictedAnswer` runs the eight-clause gate authored here, this counts how many of Hockett's design features a candidate satisfies according to published assessment. It deliberately reads *not assessed* instead of *0 of 13* for candidates nobody has scored: a silent zero was the exact defect in the hand-written `calc_language_candidates_bio_hockett_score()`, which summed columns that did not exist and so reported every candidate as scoring nothing.

schema.name: HockettVsGate
schema.Description: Names the disagreement, in English, when the eight-clause gate and Hockett's design features reach opposite conclusions. Empty when they agree or when the candidate is unassessed.
schema.formula: =IF({{HockettAssessedCount}} = 0, "", IF(AND({{PredictedAnswer}}, {{HockettYesCount}} < {{HockettAssessedCount}}), "The eight-clause gate says language; Hockett's features hold for only " & {{HockettYesCount}} & " of " & {{HockettAssessedCount}} & ".", IF(AND(NOT({{PredictedAnswer}}), {{HockettYesCount}} = {{HockettAssessedCount}}), "Hockett's features all hold, and the eight-clause gate says not a language.", "")))
schema.explanation_rich: **Where the two definitions collide, with an address.** Two candidates currently disagree. **Sign Language** passes this rulebook's eight-clause gate while Hockett's very first feature, the vocal-auditory channel, excludes it outright, which is the best-known objection to the design-features framework. **Honeybee Waggle Dance** passes the gate too, and satisfies only four of Hockett's thirteen. Neither is settled by insisting harder: both now name a specific premise a reader can go and argue with.

IsEverythingALanguage.summary_rich: The **argument itself, modelled as data.** Sixteen numbered steps (NEIAL-001 through NEIAL-016) — Motivation, PredicateSet, Definition, Witness, Counterexample, FuzzyBoundary, Refinement, Conclusion — proving two halves of a single thesis: *language can be formalized* (so a rulebook IS a language with a grammar) AND *not everything is a language* (so the formalization actually excludes things). Each step carries both a plain-English `Statement` and a logical `Formalization`, with witnesses pointing back at concrete rows in `LanguageCandidates` as evidence.

data.Name: NEIAL-001
data.Statement: To avoid the slogan 'Everything is a language', treat 'language' as a typed construct defined by testable properties (syntax, parsing, linear decoding pressure, and descriptor-role).
data.Notes: This keeps 'can be interpreted' separate from 'is a language system'.

data.Name: NEIAL-002
data.Statement: Use the repo predicates: HasSyntax, RequiresParsing, HasLinearDecodingPressure, StableOntologyReference (spelled IsOngologyDescriptor in the dataset), plus auxiliary checks like CanBeHeld and HasIdentity.
data.Formalization: Predicates: Syntax(x), Parse(x), SerializeMeaning(x), OntDesc(x), Tangible(x)
data.Notes: We preserve the dataset's field name even when misspelled to match the generated schema.

data.Name: NEIAL-003
data.Statement: Operational definition: an item x counts as a Language if it has syntax, requires parsing, serializes meaning, and functions as an ontology/descriptor system.
data.Notes: This is a deliberately 'strong' definition: it matches formal languages and many natural language representations.

data.Name: NEIAL-004
data.Statement: There exists at least one clear witness that satisfies the operational definition: English.
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=True; RequiresParsing=True; HasLinearDecodingPressure=True; IsOngologyDescriptor=True; CanBeHeld=False; HasIdentity=False; DistanceFromConcept=2; Category=Natural Language
data.Notes: If any predicate is false in your current dataset for this witness, adjust the candidate record or relax the definition.

data.Name: NEIAL-005
data.Statement: There exists at least one clear witness that satisfies the operational definition: Python.
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=True; RequiresParsing=True; HasLinearDecodingPressure=True; IsOngologyDescriptor=True; CanBeHeld=False; HasIdentity=False; DistanceFromConcept=2; Category=Formal Language
data.Notes: If any predicate is false in your current dataset for this witness, adjust the candidate record or relax the definition.

data.Name: NEIAL-006
data.Statement: Therefore, 'language' can be formalized as a computable classification boundary over explicit predicates.
data.Notes: This is the concession: language is formalizable (at least operationally).

data.Name: NEIAL-007
data.Statement: If Language(x) is defined by necessary conditions, then any x that fails at least one condition is not a language.
data.Notes: This is the standard move: a definition implies exclusions.

data.Name: NEIAL-008
data.Statement: Counterexample: a chair can be interpreted as a sign (status, design, function), but it does not constitute a language system under the operational definition.
data.Notes: This separates semiotic availability (can signify) from linguistic structure (has syntax/parsing/serialized meaning).

data.Name: NEIAL-009
data.Statement: Non-language example: A Thunderstorm can be meaningful, but meaning here is not generated by an explicit syntax+parsing+serialization descriptor system.
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=False; RequiresParsing=True; HasLinearDecodingPressure=False; IsOngologyDescriptor=False; CanBeHeld=False; HasIdentity=True; DistanceFromConcept=1; Category=Physical event
data.Notes: These are strong candidates for 'sign vehicles' rather than 'languages'.

data.Name: NEIAL-010
data.Statement: Non-language example: A Coffee Mug can be meaningful, but meaning here is not generated by an explicit syntax+parsing+serialization descriptor system.
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=False; RequiresParsing=False; HasLinearDecodingPressure=False; IsOngologyDescriptor=False; CanBeHeld=True; HasIdentity=True; DistanceFromConcept=1; Category=Physical Object
data.Notes: These are strong candidates for 'sign vehicles' rather than 'languages'.

data.Name: NEIAL-011
data.Statement: Non-language example: The Mona Lisa can be meaningful, but meaning here is not generated by an explicit syntax+parsing+serialization descriptor system.
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=False; RequiresParsing=False; HasLinearDecodingPressure=False; IsOngologyDescriptor=True; CanBeHeld=True; HasIdentity=True; DistanceFromConcept=1; Category=Physical Object
data.Notes: These are strong candidates for 'sign vehicles' rather than 'languages'.

data.Name: NEIAL-012
data.Statement: Fuzzy case: A Running App often contains embedded languages (code, UI grammars), but as an executing/interactive process it behaves like a dynamic system rather than a static serialized language artifact.
data.Formalization: Borderline(A Running App): may contain ∃y Language(y) but ¬Language(A Running App) under static-serialization criteria
data.Notes: This is where traditional semiotics' 'anything is a sign' doesn’t neatly distinguish: (1) language-as-system vs (2) meaning-making interactive processes.

data.Name: NEIAL-013
data.Statement: Fuzzy case: Running Calculator App often contains embedded languages (code, UI grammars), but as an executing/interactive process it behaves like a dynamic system rather than a static serialized language artifact.
data.Formalization: Borderline(Running Calculator App): may contain ∃y Language(y) but ¬Language(Running Calculator App) under static-serialization criteria

data.Notes: This is where traditional semiotics' 'anything is a sign' doesn’t neatly distinguish: (1) language-as-system vs (2) meaning-making interactive processes.

data.Name: NEIAL-014
data.Statement: Fuzzy case: A Game of Fortnite often contains embedded languages (code, UI grammars), but as an executing/interactive process it behaves like a dynamic system rather than a static serialized language artifact.
data.Formalization: Borderline(A Game of Fortnite): may contain ∃y Language(y) but ¬Language(A Game of Fortnite) under static-serialization criteria
data.EvidenceFromRulebook: HasSyntax=False; RequiresParsing=True; HasLinearDecodingPressure=False; IsOngologyDescriptor=False; CanBeHeld=False; HasIdentity=True; DistanceFromConcept=1; Category=Running Software
data.Notes: This is where traditional semiotics' 'anything is a sign' doesn’t neatly distinguish: (1) language-as-system vs (2) meaning-making interactive processes.

data.Name: NEIAL-015
data.Statement: Refinement: distinguish LanguageSystem (syntax/parsing/serialization descriptor) from SemioticProcess (interactive/dynamic meaning production) and from SignVehicle (object/phenomenon used as a sign).
data.Notes: This gives you a place to put running apps and games without forcing 'language' to swallow everything.

data.Name: NEIAL-016
data.Statement: Given a formalizable definition of language, not everything is a language; some things are better treated as sign vehicles or semiotic processes, with running applications as a key fuzzy region that benefits from explicit modeling.
data.Notes: This is the repo's thesis in one line.

HockettFeatures.summary_rich: **The other definition.** Charles Hockett's *design features* are the canonical linguistic answer to the same question this rulebook asks, so they belong in it as data rather than as prose. Thirteen features from 1960, plus `Prevarication`, `Reflexiveness` and `Learnability` added in 1968. `IsOriginalThirteen` separates the two. Each feature rolls up how many candidates have been assessed against it and how many satisfy it.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: The design feature's name, as Hockett gives it.

schema.name: FeatureNumber
schema.Description: Hockett's own numbering, 1 through 13, then 14 through 16 for the 1968 additions.

schema.name: Definition
schema.Description: What the feature asserts, in plain English.

schema.name: IsOriginalThirteen
schema.Description: TRUE for the thirteen features of the 1960 paper; FALSE for the three added in 1968.

schema.name: Source
schema.Description: Citation for the feature list.

schema.name: AssessmentCount
schema.Description: How many candidates have been assessed against this feature.

schema.name: YesCount
schema.Description: How many assessed candidates satisfy this feature outright.

data.Name: Vocal-Auditory Channel
data.Definition: Signals are made with the vocal tract and received by the auditory system.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Broadcast Transmission And Directional Reception
data.Definition: The signal radiates to any receiver in range, and a receiver can locate its source.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Rapid Fading
data.Definition: The signal does not persist. Unlike a track, a spoor or a written record, it is gone once transmitted and will not wait for the hearer's convenience.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Interchangeability
data.Definition: Any user who can understand a message can also produce it.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Total Feedback
data.Definition: The sender perceives everything relevant in their own signal.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Specialization
data.Definition: The signal exists in order to communicate, rather than being a side effect of some other behaviour.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Semanticity
data.Definition: Signals carry fixed associations to things and situations in the world.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Arbitrariness
data.Definition: The tie between a signal and its meaning is conventional rather than a resemblance.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Discreteness
data.Definition: The signal is built from a repertoire of distinct units, so a small deviation either switches units outright or is heard as a noisy version of the same one.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Displacement
data.Definition: Messages can be about things remote in time or space.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Productivity
data.Definition: Messages never sent before can be produced and understood.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Traditional Transmission
data.Definition: The system is learned from other users rather than inherited genetically.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Duality Of Patterning
data.Definition: A small stock of meaningless units combines into a large stock of meaningful ones.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Prevarication
data.Definition: Messages can be false, deceptive or meaningless.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Reflexiveness
data.Definition: The system can be used to communicate about itself.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

data.Name: Learnability
data.Definition: A user of one such system can learn another.
data.Source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

HockettAssessments.summary_rich: **One row per (candidate, design feature), with its receipt.** The published comparisons of Hockett's features are full of hedged cells, so `Verdict` resolves to Yes / No / Partial / Unknown while `VerbatimAssessment` preserves the source's exact wording ("Limited", "Largely yes", "Debatable", "?") and `SourceCitation` names the column it came from. `MappingNote` is filled in whenever a candidate in this rulebook maps only approximately onto the source's column, so an approximate row can never be mistaken for a direct quotation. Nothing here is assessed from intuition: a candidate with no published assessment gets no rows at all.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Logical key: the candidate and the feature being assessed.

schema.name: LanguageCandidate
schema.Description: FK to the candidate being assessed.

schema.name: HockettFeature
schema.Description: FK to the design feature being applied.

schema.name: Verdict
schema.Description: Yes, No, Partial or Unknown. Partial and Unknown exist because the published assessments hedge, and flattening a hedge into a boolean would bury a judgement call in the data.

schema.name: VerbatimAssessment
schema.Description: The source's exact wording for this cell, so every resolution to Verdict stays auditable.

schema.name: SourceCitation
schema.Description: Where this cell came from, including which column.

schema.name: MappingNote
schema.Description: Empty when this candidate corresponds exactly to the source's column. Otherwise, how the two differ and how far the row should be trusted.

schema.name: IsYesFlag
schema.Description: 1 when the verdict is an outright Yes, else 0. Summed by the rollups on LanguageCandidates and HockettFeatures.

data.Name: 02b-customize-functions.sql
data.Title: Customize Functions
data.SQLCode:
-- Prediction Fail: Returns TRUE when predicted_answer doesn't match is_language
DROP FUNCTION calc_language_candidates_question;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.calc_language_candidates_question(p_language_candidate_id text)
 RETURNS text
 LANGUAGE plpgsql
 STABLE SECURITY DEFINER
AS $function$
BEGIN
  RETURN ('Is ' || (SELECT NULLIF(name, '''') FROM language_candidates WHERE language_candidate_id = p_language_candidate_id) || ' a language?')::text;
END;
$function$;

-- calc_language_candidates_bio_hockett_score was removed here. It summed eleven
-- bio_has_* columns that were never declared in the rulebook, so it could only
-- error when called or report every candidate as scoring zero. Hockett's design
-- features are now first-class rulebook data (HockettFeatures,
-- HockettAssessments) and LanguageCandidates.HockettScore is computed from them.
-- The DROP is explicit because a check-add rebuild does not remove a function
-- that has merely stopped being created.
DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS calc_language_candidates_bio_hockett_score(text);

__meta__.Description: Project-level metadata that travels with the rulebook: tagline, motif, narrative descriptions, substrate list, signature rows, etc. One row per metadata key. Use ValueType to interpret StringValue vs JsonValue.

schema.name: MetaKey
schema.Description: The metadata key (e.g. 'tagline', 'motif_palette', 'substrates'). Unique within the table.

schema.name: Name
schema.Description: Identifier for this metadata entry. Mirrors MetaKey so the row is addressable by Name like every other table.

schema.name: ValueType
schema.Description: How to interpret the value columns: 'string' (use StringValue), 'object' (parse JsonValue as JSON object), 'array' (parse JsonValue as JSON array).

schema.name: StringValue
schema.Description: Plain string value. Populated when ValueType == 'string'; null otherwise.

schema.name: JsonValue
schema.Description: JSON-encoded value. Populated when ValueType == 'object' or 'array'; null when ValueType == 'string'.

data.Name: tagline
data.StringValue: Anything you can model as a rulebook is — by construction — a language with a grammar.

data.Name: description_rich
data.StringValue: This isn't a business app — it's a **self-referential proof**. The rulebook contains a taxonomy of candidate languages (English, Python, OWL, a coffee mug, a thunderstorm, honeybee waggle dance, Nicaraguan Sign Language) and an *operational definition* of *language* expressed as an eight-clause formula. The same rulebook contains the sixteen-step argument that the operational definition is itself coherent — Definition, Witnesses, Counterexamples, Fuzzy Boundaries, Conclusion. So the artefact you're reading **is** the thing it's arguing about: a structured ontology with a grammar, computing its own classifications, auditing its own disagreements. The CMCC conjecture, demonstrated by self-application.

data.Name: use_cases
data.JsonValue: ["**Watch the operational definition fire.** Open *English* and see `PredictedAnswer` resolve to TRUE through its eight-clause AND.
